report.source_text: Given the persistence and progressive nature of the lesion during the 3 weeks, with associated pruritus and with an inflammatory skin appearance, treatment was initiated with systemic corticosteroid therapy - hydrocortisone hemisuccinate 200 mg/day for 7 days, and loratadine 10 mg 2 times a day. Topical medication with dermatocorticosteroids and emollients were used with partial remission of the lesions after 7 days (Fig. 2). Two weeks after the admission into the Infectious Diseases Department, the patient was discharged with partial resolution of the skin lesions, without respiratory manifestations, and with a negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR from nasal and pharyngeal swabs.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 54-year-old female presented with a 3-week history of an extremely pruritic erythematous-squamous rash, initially on the trunk and upper limbs, extending to the lower limbs. One week prior to rash onset, she experienced respiratory symptoms. Dermatological examination revealed an oval erythematous squamous plaque (herald patch) in the right supraclavicular area, and disseminated oval erythematous-papulosquamous lesions (0.5-1 cm) with a linear pattern, associated with pruritus and centrifugal progressive extension. The eruption did not involve soles, palms, or the facial area. A SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR test was positive. Syphilis serology and HIV antibodies tests were negative. Laboratory tests showed elevated ESR and LDH, but other parameters and pulmonary radiography were normal. Treatment with systemic corticosteroids, loratadine, topical corticosteroids, and emollients led to partial remission of lesions after 7 days. Two weeks post-admission, the patient was discharged with partial resolution of skin lesions, no respiratory manifestations, and a negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR.
